cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: Criminal courts deal with offences against the state; civil courts deal with disputes between individuals or organisations

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: The Magistrates' Court hears 95% of criminal cases — summary offences and either-way offences

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: The Crown Court hears indictable offences (serious crimes) and appeals from the Magistrates' Court

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: The High Court hears the most serious civil cases, divided into three divisions: Queen's Bench, Chancery and Family

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: The County Court handles most civil claims including contract disputes, tort and debt recovery

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: The Court of Appeal (Criminal and Civil Divisions) hears appeals on points of law and sentence

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: The Supreme Court is the highest court — it hears appeals on points of law of general public importance

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: Tribunals resolve specialist disputes (employment, immigration, tax) more informally than courts

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: The Youth Court handles criminal cases involving defendants aged 10-17

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: The court hierarchy ensures that lower courts follow higher courts' decisions under the doctrine of precedent

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: Appeal routes allow cases to be reviewed by higher courts if there are errors of law or unduly harsh sentences

cards.front: Recall a key point about Courts & Court Structure
cards.back: Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) — mediation, arbitration and negotiation — resolves disputes outside court

cards.front: What should you know about gcse law exam tips — courts & court structure?
cards.back: 1. For Courts & Court Structure questions, identify the relevant area of law and state the legal principles clearly 2. Apply legal rules to the facts of the scenario — don't just state the law 3. When evaluating, consider both the effectiveness and fairness of legal rules 4. Reference relevant cases and statutes when discussing Courts & Court Structure 5. Consider reform proposals and alternative approaches where relevant
